summary: Documents version 2 of the Internet Group Management Protocol, which hosts use to tell nearby routers which multicast groups they belong to. It updates RFC 1112. Version 2 adds improvements such as leaving a group more quickly.

eli5.summary: When you want to watch a group broadcast, you tell the nearest router you are joining. This is how you raise your hand to join or leave.

questions: how do hosts join multicast groups
how do hosts join a multicast group
what is the igmp leave group message
subtitle: How hosts tell their local multicast routers which groups they want, and how they say goodbye quickly.

tldr.problem: Multicast routers need to know which groups have listeners on each attached network, and IGMP version 1 gave no way to report that the last member had left, so traffic kept flowing until a timeout.
tldr.mechanism: A querier router asks the network which groups have members, hosts answer with randomly delayed reports (suppressing duplicates), and a new Leave Group message lets routers check quickly whether anyone is left.
tldr.outcome: IGMPv2 updates RFC 1112 and speeds up leave latency. It has since been updated by RFC 3376 and RFC 9776.

today: RFC 2236 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1112, and it has itself been updated by RFC 3376 and RFC 9776.

sections.title: What IGMP Does
sections.content:
The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is used by IP hosts to report their multicast group memberships to any immediately neighboring multicast routers. This memo describes only the use of IGMP between hosts and routers. It updates RFC 1112.

Like ICMP, IGMP is an integral part of IP, and it is required of all hosts wishing to receive IP multicasts. IGMP messages travel inside IP datagrams with IP protocol number 2. Every message in this document is sent with IP TTL 1 and carries the IP Router Alert option from RFC 2113.

The headline improvement over version 1 is that group membership termination can be reported quickly to the routing protocol. That matters for high-bandwidth groups and for subnets where membership changes often.
sections.eli5: IGMP is how a computer tells the nearby router, 'I want to hear this group.' It only talks to the router next door, never farther.

sections.title: The IGMP Message
sections.content:
All IGMP messages that hosts care about share one 8-octet layout: a one-octet Type, a one-octet Max Response Time, a 16-bit Checksum and a 32-bit Group Address.

There are three message types for host-router interaction: 0x11 Membership Query, 0x16 Version 2 Membership Report and 0x17 Leave Group. A fourth, 0x12, is the Version 1 Membership Report, kept for backward compatibility. A Query is either a General Query (group address zero, asking which groups have members) or a Group-Specific Query (asking about one group). Unrecognized types are silently ignored.

Max Response Time is meaningful only in Queries. It is given in units of 1/10 second, and it is set to zero and ignored in all other messages. The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the whole IGMP message, and it MUST be computed when sending and verified when receiving. A receiver MUST ignore anything past the first 8 octets, but the checksum still covers the whole IP payload.
sections.eli5: Every IGMP note is a tiny form with four boxes: what kind of note it is, how long to wait before answering, a scramble check, and which group it is about.

sections.title: Querying, Reporting and Leaving
sections.content:
For each attached network a multicast router is either the Querier or a Non-Querier. All routers start as Querier. If a router hears a Query from a router with a lower IP address, it MUST become a Non-Querier, and it resumes the Querier role if it has heard no Query for the Other Querier Present Interval. The Querier periodically sends a General Query to the all-systems group (224.0.0.1), and on startup it SHOULD send several closely spaced ones.

When a host receives a General Query, it starts a separate random delay timer for each group it belongs to, chosen from the range (0, Max Response Time]. When a timer expires, the host multicasts a Report to that group with TTL 1. If it first hears another host's Report for the same group, it stops its timer and stays quiet, which suppresses duplicate reports. The router only needs to know that at least one member exists, and each Report refreshes its membership timer.

A host that joins a group should immediately send an unsolicited Report, and it is recommended to repeat it once or twice after short delays in case it was lost.

When a host leaves a group and it was the last host to answer a Query for that group, it SHOULD send a Leave Group message to the all-routers group (224.0.0.2). On receiving it, the Querier sends Group-Specific Queries, and if no Report answers them, it assumes the group has no local members. Non-Queriers MUST ignore Leave Group messages.
sections.eli5: The router asks, 'Who wants group X?' Everyone waits a random moment, and the first to answer speaks for all, so the router is not buried in identical answers. When the last one leaves, the router double-checks before turning the group off.

sections.title: Living with IGMPv1
sections.content:
On a subnet whose Querier still runs IGMPv1, a host MUST treat a Query with Max Response Time 0 as a value of 100 (10 seconds), and it MUST keep a per-interface state variable recording whether an IGMPv1 query was heard within the Version 1 Router Present Timeout (400 seconds). While an IGMPv1 router is present, the host sends Version 1 Reports, and it MAY skip Leave Group messages.

An IGMPv2 router that shares a subnet with an IGMPv1 router MUST use IGMPv1, and this has to be set by administrators because there is no reliable way to detect IGMPv1 routers dynamically. In that mode it sends Queries with Max Response Time 0 and ignores Leave Group messages. By default the configuration MUST be IGMPv2.

For IGMPv1 hosts, a host MUST allow its Report to be suppressed by either a Version 1 or a Version 2 Report. A router that hears a Version 1 Report starts a timer equal to the Group Membership Interval and MUST ignore Leave Group messages for that group while it runs.
sections.eli5: Old and new versions have to share a room. The new ones speak the old language when an old one is around, and they give up the fast 'goodbye' trick that the old ones would not understand.

sections.title: Host and Router State Machines
sections.content:
For each group on each interface, a host is in one of three states: Non-Member, Delaying Member (a report timer is running) or Idle Member (a member with no timer). Joining sends a Report, sets a flag and starts a timer. A received Query starts the timer, and a Report from another host stops it and clears the flag. When the timer expires the host sends a Report and sets the flag. Leaving sends a Leave only if the flag is set. The all-systems group is a special case: the host is always Idle for it and never reports it.

A router tracks each group on each network in one of four states: No Members Present, Members Present, Version 1 Members Present and Checking Membership. A Report moves it to Members Present and tells the routing protocol that members exist. A Leave moves it to Checking Membership, where it retransmits Group-Specific Queries. If the timer expires without a Report, the routing protocol is told the group has no members.
sections.eli5: A kid in the group is either not in it, in it and about to answer, or in it and quietly waiting. The router keeps a similar little checklist for every group.

sections.title: Timers and Default Values
sections.content:
Most timers are configurable, but non-default settings MUST be consistent among all routers on a link. The Robustness Variable tunes for expected packet loss: IGMP is robust to (Robustness Variable minus 1) losses. It MUST NOT be zero and SHOULD NOT be one, and the default is 2.

The Query Interval defaults to 125 seconds, and the Query Response Interval (the Max Response Time in periodic General Queries) defaults to 100, which is 10 seconds. The Group Membership Interval MUST be the Robustness Variable times the Query Interval, plus one Query Response Interval. The Last Member Query Interval defaults to 10 (1 second), and tuning it changes the leave latency. The Unsolicited Report Interval defaults to 10 seconds.

The RFC also summarizes destinations: General Queries go to 224.0.0.1, Group-Specific Queries and Reports go to the group concerned, and Leave messages go to 224.0.0.2. Hosts MUST send Leaves to the all-routers address to comply, but routers SHOULD still accept Leaves addressed to the group, for older implementations.
sections.eli5: There are stopwatches for how often to ask, how long to wait to answer and how long before giving up on a group. The defaults are sensible, and you can change them for a noisy network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a forged message of each type. A forged Query from a lower IP address makes the forger the Querier; if it then ignores Leave messages, traffic might flow to groups with no members for up to the Group Membership Interval. A forged Report can make routers think a group has members. A forged Version 1 Report can put a router into Version 1 Members Present state so it ignores Leaves. A forged Leave only causes extra Group-Specific Queries and cannot cause loss of desired traffic.

The suggested defenses are to ignore Reports and Leaves whose source address does not belong to a subnet assigned to the receiving interface, or to ignore them if they lack the Router Alert option. For Version 1 Reports, routers can also be given a switch to ignore them completely, which breaks automatic compatibility with Version 1 hosts.
sections.eli5: Someone could pretend to be a classmate and raise a hand or say 'I'm leaving.' The fixes are checking that the voice really comes from inside the room.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: 0x11 Query, 0x16 v2 Report, 0x17 Leave Group, 0x12 v1 Report.

fields.name: Max Resp Time
fields.desc: Used in Queries only, in units of 1/10 second.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum of the whole IGMP message.

fields.name: Group Address
fields.desc: Zero in a General Query; otherwise the group concerned.
